questions.title: Lipid soluble substance crosses cell membrane through the phospholipid bilayer
questions.question: A lipid soluble substance can pass the cell membrane through

explanations.A: Correct. Simple diffusion moves a lipid-soluble substance passively down its concentration gradient. It crosses directly through the lipid bilayer itself, without needing a channel or carrier protein at all. The molecule's own lipid solubility is what lets it dissolve into and cross the membrane's phospholipid core.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Protein channels are the route for ions and other charged or polar substances that cannot dissolve into the lipid bilayer, not for lipid-soluble molecules, which cross the bilayer directly instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Carrier proteins mediate facilitated diffusion and active transport of specific, usually larger or polar, molecules; a small lipid-soluble substance does not need a carrier since it can cross the bilayer directly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Lipid carrier" is not the standard teaching mechanism for a lipid-soluble substance crossing the membrane -- the substance's own solubility in the bilayer is what lets it cross, without a distinct carrier molecule.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: State that a lipid-soluble substance crosses the cell membrane directly through the phospholipid bilayer.

questions.title: Sodium down its gradient needs a protein channel
questions.question: Sodium ions to pass through the cell membrane from high to low concentration, it needs

explanations.A: Correct. Sodium moving down its own concentration gradient, from high to low, is simple diffusion. Na+ is a charged ion that cannot cross the lipid bilayer directly, so it needs a protein channel, a non-gated or gated pore, to pass through. It does not need a carrier or any energy input for this passive, gradient-driven movement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A carrier protein is needed for facilitated diffusion of larger, uncharged molecules such as glucose, not for an ion moving down its gradient through a channel.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Movement down a concentration gradient (diffusion, whether simple or facilitated) is passive and does not require ATP; ATP is needed only when a substance moves against its gradient (active transport).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neither ATP nor a carrier is needed here -- Na+ moving down its gradient through a protein channel is a passive process.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: State that an ion moving down its concentration gradient needs a protein channel, not a carrier or ATP.

questions.title: Osmosis: water moves from low to high solute concentration
questions.question: Water pass from area of low solute to area of high solute concentration by

explanations.A: Incorrect. Simple diffusion describes a solute moving down its own concentration gradient, not water moving in response to a solute gradient -- that specific water movement is named osmosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Facilitated diffusion requires a carrier protein for a specific solute; it is not the term for water crossing a membrane along an osmotic gradient.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Exocytosis is the process of a cell secreting material by fusing a vesicle with the plasma membrane, unrelated to water movement along a solute gradient.
explanations.D: Correct. Osmosis is the diffusion of water, from a region of high water concentration (low solute concentration) to a region of low water concentration (high solute concentration). It happens across a membrane permeable to water but not to the solute. This is exactly the movement this question describes.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: Define osmosis as water moving from a region of low solute concentration to a region of high solute concentration.

questions.title: Oxygen is transported from blood to cells by simple diffusion
questions.question: Oxygen is transported from blood to the cells by

explanations.A: Correct. Oxygen is small and lipid-soluble, so it crosses cell membranes by simple diffusion directly through the lipid bilayer. It moves passively down its concentration gradient from blood, where O2 is higher, into the cells, where O2 is lower. This crossing needs no carrier, channel or energy input.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Facilitated diffusion needs a specific carrier protein, unlike O2, which crosses the bilayer directly because of its lipid solubility.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Active transport moves a substance against its concentration gradient using energy; O2 moves down its gradient passively, which is the definition of diffusion, not active transport.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osmosis specifically describes water movement along a solute gradient, not the diffusion of a dissolved gas such as O2.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: State that oxygen is transported from blood to cells by simple diffusion.

questions.title: Glucose is transported from blood to cells by facilitated diffusion
questions.question: glucose is transported from blood to the cells by

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glucose is too large and polar to cross the lipid bilayer directly by simple diffusion; it needs a carrier protein.
explanations.B: Correct. Glucose is too large and polar to diffuse directly through the lipid bilayer, so it depends on a specific carrier protein (e.g. GLUT transporters) that binds it and carries it across, still moving passively down its concentration gradient -- this carrier-mediated, passive, gradient-following movement is exactly what defines facilitated diffusion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Moving glucose from blood into most cells down its concentration gradient does not require energy, so it is classed as facilitated diffusion, not active transport, under ordinary physiological conditions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osmosis specifically describes water movement along a solute gradient, not the transport of glucose itself.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: State that glucose is transported from blood to cells by facilitated diffusion.

questions.title: Rate of diffusion is affected by concentration gradient
questions.question: the rate of diffusion is affected by

options.B: Amount of ATP in the cell

explanations.A: Correct. The concentration gradient across the membrane is the driving force of diffusion. A steeper gradient produces a faster net rate of diffusion. This is because diffusion is fundamentally the passive movement of a substance down that gradient, so a bigger difference means a bigger net flux.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Diffusion (simple or facilitated) is a passive process and does not depend on ATP; ATP availability is relevant to active transport, not diffusion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mitochondrial number relates to the cell's capacity for ATP production, which is not a factor in a passive process such as diffusion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Blood pressure is not a determinant of the rate of diffusion across a cell membrane, which depends instead on factors such as the concentration gradient, membrane area, thickness and the substance's lipid solubility and molecular weight.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: State that the rate of diffusion is affected by the concentration gradient across the membrane.

questions.title: Transport needing a carrier and energy is active transport
questions.question: the type of transport that needs a carrier and energy is

explanations.A: Incorrect. Simple diffusion needs neither a carrier nor energy -- it is a passive movement directly through the bilayer or a channel.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Facilitated diffusion needs a carrier protein but not energy, since it still moves the substance down its concentration gradient.
explanations.C: Correct. Active transport is defined by needing both a specific carrier protein and energy derived from ATP, which the carrier hydrolyses through its own ATPase activity. This combination lets it move a substance against its electrochemical gradient, something diffusion cannot do. This need for carrier plus energy input together is exactly what distinguishes active transport from either form of diffusion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osmosis is the passive diffusion of water and needs neither a carrier nor energy.

questions.learning_objective: Identify active transport as the transport type needing both a carrier and energy.

questions.title: Na-glucose cotransport is an example of secondary active transport
questions.question: an example of secondary active transport is

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Na+-K+ pump is the classic example of primary, not secondary, active transport -- it hydrolyses ATP directly itself.
explanations.B: Correct. Na-glucose cotransport (a symport) rides the Na+ gradient that the Na+-K+ pump has already built. It spends no ATP of its own. This is exactly the definition of secondary active transport: moving glucose alongside Na+ using the energy stored in Na+'s own electrochemical gradient, rather than spending fresh ATP directly.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Na+ diffusion (movement down its own gradient) is a passive process, not active transport at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glucose diffusion (facilitated diffusion) is also passive, following glucose's own concentration gradient without energy input, not an active transport process.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Na-glucose cotransport as an example of secondary active transport.

questions.title: Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion by needing a carrier
questions.question: facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion in that

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neither facilitated nor simple diffusion needs energy -- both are passive processes that follow the concentration gradient; the defining difference between them is the need for a carrier, not energy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is facilitated diffusion, not simple diffusion, that needs a carrier protein -- simple diffusion crosses the bilayer or a channel directly, without one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Simple diffusion is passive and does not need energy; needing energy is a feature of active transport, not either form of diffusion.
explanations.D: Correct. Facilitated diffusion depends on a specific carrier protein that binds the substance and carries it across the membrane. Simple diffusion, by contrast, crosses the bilayer or a channel directly, without any carrier. This need for a carrier is exactly what distinguishes facilitated from simple diffusion, since both remain equally passive and gradient-driven otherwise.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: State that facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion in needing a carrier protein, not in needing energy.

questions.title: Rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to molecular weight
questions.question: the rate of diffusion of a substance is inversely proportionate with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The rate of diffusion is directly, not inversely, proportional to the concentration gradient -- a steeper gradient speeds diffusion up, it does not slow it down.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The rate of diffusion is directly, not inversely, proportional to temperature -- higher temperature increases molecular motion and speeds diffusion up.
explanations.C: Incorrect. For a lipid-soluble substance, the rate of diffusion is directly, not inversely, proportional to its lipid solubility -- greater solubility in the bilayer speeds diffusion up.
explanations.D: Correct. Larger, heavier molecules diffuse more slowly than smaller, lighter ones for a given gradient. The rate of diffusion is therefore inversely proportional to the substance's molecular weight. This is the one factor among those listed that slows diffusion as it increases, rather than speeding it up.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: State that the rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to the diffusing substance's molecular weight.

questions.title: Active transport necessary for movement against electrochemical gradient
questions.question: Regarding transport across the cell membrane:

options.A: facilitated diffusion is an energy requiring process.
options.B: active transport is necessary for the movement of molecules against electrochemical gradient.
options.C: water soluble substances of large molecular size diffuse through the phospholipids.
options.D: only fat soluble substances can pass easily through the pores created by the integral proteins.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Facilitated diffusion is a passive process, following the concentration gradient just as simple diffusion does; it does not require energy, unlike active transport.
explanations.B: Correct. Moving a substance against its electrochemical gradient, from a region of lower to higher electrochemical potential, is precisely what active transport is needed for. Diffusion, whether simple or facilitated, can only move a substance down its gradient. Overcoming that gradient therefore requires the carrier-plus-energy mechanism of active transport instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Large, water-soluble substances cannot diffuse through the lipid phospholipid core of the membrane; they need a protein channel or carrier, since the lipid bilayer excludes large polar molecules.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Protein channels (formed by integral proteins) are the route for water-soluble ions and small polar substances, not specifically fat-soluble substances -- fat-soluble substances instead cross the lipid bilayer directly, without needing a channel at all.

questions.learning_objective: State that active transport is necessary for moving a substance against its electrochemical gradient.

field_notes.pendingConcept: CON-NEU-75498C01CA1857, same pending Kasr 103-BMS-physiology concept as Q109/Q110 above.

questions.title: Diffusion decreases if membrane thickness increases
questions.question: Diffusion of solutes across semi-permeable membrane will decrease if there is an increase in the:

options.C: Solute concentration difference across the membrane.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Increasing membrane area increases, not decreases, the rate of diffusion, since it gives more surface across which molecules can cross.
explanations.B: Correct. A thicker membrane increases the distance a diffusing particle must travel. Diffusion rate is inversely related to that distance, so the further a molecule must diffuse, the slower the net rate of crossing. Increasing membrane thickness therefore decreases the rate of diffusion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Increasing the concentration difference (gradient) increases, not decreases, the driving force and so the rate of diffusion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increasing temperature increases molecular kinetic energy and so increases, not decreases, the rate of diffusion.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: State that diffusion across a membrane decreases as membrane thickness increases.

questions.title: Rate of diffusion increases if lipid solubility increases
questions.question: The rate of diffusion of a particle across a membrane will increase if:

options.A: The concentration gradient for the particle decreases.
options.B: The size of the particle increases.
options.C: The lipid solubility of the particle increases.
options.D: The area of the membrane decreases.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A decreasing concentration gradient reduces, not increases, the driving force for diffusion, so the rate would fall, not rise.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A larger particle diffuses more slowly, not faster -- the rate of diffusion is inversely related to particle size (and molecular weight).
explanations.C: Correct. For a substance that crosses the membrane by dissolving into the lipid bilayer, greater lipid solubility means it partitions into the bilayer more readily. It then moves through that lipid core more easily too. Both effects together increase the rate of diffusion as lipid solubility rises.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A smaller membrane area gives less surface across which the particle can cross, decreasing, not increasing, the rate of diffusion.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: State that the rate of diffusion increases as the diffusing particle's lipid solubility increases.

field_notes.pendingConcept: CON-NEU-1D5DC2D67A5291, same pending Kasr 103-BMS-physiology concept as Q103-113/Q118 above.

questions.title: Ions pass freely through protein channels
questions.question: Regarding the transport mechanisms across the cellular membrane:

options.A: facilitated diffusion is an active process.
options.B: ions pass freely through protein channels.
options.C: Na+-K+ pump is an example of secondary active transport.
options.D: counter transport is transporting 2 molecules in the same direction.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Facilitated diffusion is a passive, not active, process -- it needs a carrier but no energy, and still follows the concentration gradient.
explanations.B: Correct. Ions cross the membrane through protein channels, which are non-gated or gated pores. Once a channel is open, ions pass through it relatively freely, moving down their electrochemical gradient. This is unlike a carrier, which must bind and release the substance in a slower cycle rather than simply letting it pass.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Na+-K+ pump is the classic example of primary, not secondary, active transport -- it hydrolyses ATP directly itself, rather than riding a gradient another pump has already built.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Counter transport (antiport) by definition moves two substances in opposite directions across the membrane, not the same direction -- moving two substances the same way is symport (cotransport), not counter transport.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: State that ions pass relatively freely through protein channels, distinguishing this from facilitated diffusion's carrier dependence and from primary vs secondary active transport.

questions.title: Rate of diffusion, EXCEPT: does not depend on ATP as energy source
questions.question: The rate of diffusion of a solute across a membrane depends on all, EXCEPT:

options.A: Total area of membrane exposed to the solute
options.B: Electrical gradient for the solute across the membrane.
options.C: ATP as a source of energy.
options.D: Concentration gradient for the solute across the membrane.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception -- this is a true determinant. A larger membrane area exposed to the solute increases the rate of diffusion, since more surface is available for crossing.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception -- this is a true determinant. For a charged solute, the electrical gradient (part of the overall electrochemical gradient) contributes to the driving force for diffusion, alongside the concentration gradient.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is the exception (the false determinant). Diffusion is a passive process and does not depend on ATP as an energy source. ATP is needed instead for active transport, which moves a substance against its gradient. Diffusion moves a substance down its gradient, which needs no such energy input.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception -- this is a true determinant. The concentration gradient is the primary driving force for diffusion -- a steeper gradient increases the rate.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: Identify that the rate of diffusion does not depend on ATP, unlike active transport.

field_notes.pendingConcept: CON-NEU-1D5DC2D67A5291, same pending Kasr 103-BMS-physiology concept as above.

questions.title: Osmosis, EXCEPT: is movement of water, not solute, across the membrane
questions.question: Concerning osmosis across selectively permeable membrane, all are true, EXCEPT:

options.A: it is the movement of solute across a semi-permeable membrane from an area in which it is in low concentration to an area in which it is in high concentration.
options.B: it is caused by a concentration difference of water.
options.C: the osmotic pressure is the amount of pressure required to stop osmosis completely.
options.D: the osmotic pressure is determined by the number of particles per unit volume of fluid.

explanations.A: Correct -- this is the exception (the false statement). Osmosis is the movement of water, not solute, across a semi-permeable membrane. It moves from an area of low solute (high water) concentration to an area of high solute (low water) concentration. This statement misdescribes osmosis as solute movement, describing instead what would be solute diffusion in the opposite direction.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Osmosis is driven by a concentration difference of water (equivalently, of solute) across the membrane.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Osmotic pressure is defined as the pressure that must be applied to stop osmosis completely.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Osmotic pressure depends on the number of particles per unit volume of fluid (osmolarity), not their mass or chemical identity.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: Identify that osmosis is the movement of water, not solute, across a semi-permeable membrane.

questions.title: Lipid bilayer allows free diffusion of O2 and alcohol
questions.question: The lipid bilayer of the cell membrane:

options.B: allows free diffusion of oxygen and alcohol through the membrane.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lipid bilayer is composed mainly, but not entirely, of phospholipids -- it also contains cholesterol and other lipids, alongside the embedded membrane proteins.
explanations.B: Correct. Small, lipid-soluble molecules such as oxygen and alcohol dissolve readily into the lipid bilayer. They then diffuse freely through it, without needing a channel or carrier. Their lipid solubility is what lets them cross the hydrophobic core directly, unlike charged or polar substances.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lipid bilayer itself is not highly permeable to Na+ -- a charged ion such as sodium needs a protein channel to cross, since it cannot dissolve into the hydrophobic lipid core.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Likewise, the lipid bilayer itself is not the route for K+ -- potassium, also a charged ion, crosses through dedicated protein channels (leak channels at rest), not by dissolving into the lipid bilayer.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: State that the lipid bilayer allows free diffusion of lipid-soluble molecules such as oxygen and alcohol, unlike charged ions such as Na+ and K+.

field_notes.pendingConcept: CON-NEU-1D5DC2D67A5291, same pending Kasr 103-BMS-physiology concept as above.

questions.title: Facilitated diffusion stops when all carrier binding sites are filled
questions.question: Facilitated diffusion:

options.A: needs a constant supply of energy.
options.C: stops when all the binding sites of the carrier protein are filled.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Facilitated diffusion is a passive process and does not need energy -- it still follows the concentration gradient, unlike active transport.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Facilitated diffusion can only move a substance down, not against, its electrochemical gradient -- moving against a gradient requires active transport.
explanations.C: Correct. Facilitated diffusion depends on a finite number of carrier protein binding sites. Once all of those binding sites are occupied, the carriers are saturated. The rate of transport then cannot increase further no matter how much the concentration gradient rises, so transport effectively plateaus once the carriers are fully occupied.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Like simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion can only move a substance down its concentration gradient, not against it -- moving against the gradient again requires active transport.

questions.subtopic: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
questions.learning_objective: State that facilitated diffusion saturates (plateaus) once all the carrier protein's binding sites are filled.
